pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
> 🔤 **Strand 2 — Algebra**
Using letters and symbols to describe patterns, relationships and unknown quantities.

> 🎯 **Content standard** (B7.2.3)
- B7.2.3.1 — Demonstrate an understanding of linear equations of the form x + a = b (where a and b are integers) by modelling problems as a linear equation and solving the problems concretely, pictorially and symbolically.

> 🎯 **In this chapter you will learn to:**
- translate word problems into linear equations and write word problems for given equations
- use flag diagrams and inverse operations to solve equations
- model and solve equations with a balance, counters and algebra tiles
- solve linear equations in one variable symbolically

pages.title: Writing equations from word problems
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Translate word problems to linear equations in one variable and vice versa.
Curriculum indicator B7.2.3.1.1
> 🔑 **Key idea: Equation** — An **equation** is a statement that two expressions are equal, e.g. 2x − 7 = 41. To **solve** an equation means to find the value of the unknown that makes the statement true. That value is the **solution**.
## Flag diagrams and inverse operations
A **flag diagram** shows the operations done to the unknown, in order. To solve the equation we move **backwards** through the diagram doing the **inverse** (opposite) operation at each step: + ↔ −, × ↔ ÷.
## ✏️ Example 7.1
Think of a number, double it and subtract 7. The result is 41. What was the original number?
**Solution**
[[fig:m7-f28]]
Figure 7.1: Flag diagram for 2x − 7 = 41 and its inverse
2x − 7 = 41
Add 7 to both sides: 2x = 48
Divide both sides by 2: **x = 24**
Check: 2 × 24 − 7 = 48 − 7 = 41 ✓
## ✏️ Example 7.2
Write an equation for each problem and solve it.
a) The sum of the ages of two friends is 25, and the older one is 4 times the age of the younger one.
b) Adaako and Afrakoma shared 40 oranges. Afrakoma had 6 more than Adaako.
**Solution**
a) Let the younger friend's age be x. Then the older one's age is 4x.
4x + x = 25 ⟹ 5x = 25 ⟹ **x = 5**
The younger friend is 5 years old and the older one is 20.
b) Let Adaako's share be x. Then Afrakoma's share is x + 6.
x + (x + 6) = 40 ⟹ 2x + 6 = 40 ⟹ 2x = 34 ⟹ **x = 17**
Adaako had 17 oranges and Afrakoma had 23.

pages.title: Example 7.3
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 7.3
Write a word problem for each equation. a) x + x = 15 b) 2x − 4 = 12 c) [[2/3]]x = 4
**Solution**
a) The sum of two equal numbers is 15. (Each number is 7.5.)
b) When 4 is taken away from 2 times a certain number, the result is 12. (The number is 8.)
c) Two-thirds of a certain number is 4. (The number is 6.)

pages.title: Solving equations with concrete materials
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Model and solve linear equations using concrete materials (e.g. counters and integer tiles) and describe the process orally and symbolically.
Curriculum indicator B7.2.3.1.2
An equation is like a **balance**. Whatever we do to one side we must do to the other side to keep it balanced.
## ✏️ Example 7.4
Solve x + 3 = 7 using a balance.
**Solution**
[[fig:m7-f29]]
Figure 7.2: A bag of x counters and 3 counters balance 7 counters
Remove 3 counters from each side. The bag balances 4 counters.
x + 3 = 7
x + 3 − 3 = 7 − 3
**x = 4**
## ✏️ Example 7.5
Solve a) 3x + 1 = x + 5 b) 3y + 4 = 2y + 8
**Solution**
a) Remove x from both sides, then 1 from both sides, then share equally:
3x + 1 − x = x + 5 − x → 2x + 1 = 5
2x + 1 − 1 = 5 − 1 → 2x = 4
**x = 2**
b) Remove 2y from both sides, then 4 from both sides:
3y + 4 − 2y = 2y + 8 − 2y → y + 4 = 8
**y = 4**
## ✏️ Example 7.6
In each balance the mass of one shape is given. Find the mass of the other shape.
[[fig:m7-f30]]
Figure 7.3: Shapes on balances
**Solution**
a) Let a triangle weigh t grams. 2t + 10 = t + 25. Remove one triangle from each side: t + 10 = 25, so **t = 15 g**.
b) Each rhombus weighs 12 g. Pentagon + 1 rhombus = 3 rhombuses, so pentagon = 2 rhombuses = **24 g**.
c) Two circles balance a square, and a square and a circle balance a triangle. The three shapes together weigh 30 g. Replace each shape by circles: square = 2 circles, triangle = 3 circles. So 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 circles = 30 g, giving **circle = 5 g, square = 10 g, triangle = 15 g**.

pages.title: Example 7.7
pages.body:
> 🧪 **Activity 7.1 — Balancing with real objects**
Use a simple balance (a ruler on a pencil, or a scale) with identical bottle tops as unit masses and small closed envelopes containing an equal, hidden number of bottle tops as "x". Set up 2x + 1 = 7, then remove equal amounts from both sides until one envelope is alone. Open the envelopes to check your answer. Describe each step aloud to your group.
**Indicator B7.2.3.1.3** Model linear equations, then write mathematical expressions and describe the process of solving the equation using algebra tiles.
> 🔑 **Key idea: Algebra tiles** — A long tile represents **x** and a small square tile represents **1**. A shaded (red) small tile represents **−1**. A pair made of +1 and −1 is a **zero pair** — it can be added or removed without changing the value.
## ✏️ Example 7.7
Use algebra tiles to model and solve a) 2x + 3 = 7 b) 3x − 2 = 10
**Solution**
[[fig:m7-f31]]
Figure 7.4: Algebra tile models
a) Remove 3 unit tiles from each side: 2x = 4. Share the 4 units equally between the 2 x-tiles: **x = 2**.
b) Add 2 positive unit tiles to each side; on the left they make zero pairs with the −1 tiles: 3x = 12. Share 12 units among 3 x-tiles: **x = 4**.

pages.title: Solving linear equations symbolically
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Solve linear equations in one variable.
Curriculum indicator B7.2.3.1.4
> 🔑 **Key idea: Rules for solving** — You may **add** the same number to both sides, **subtract** the same number from both sides, **multiply** both sides by the same non-zero number or **divide** both sides by the same non-zero number. Aim to get the unknown alone on one side.
## ✏️ Example 7.8
Solve 3x + 5 = 20.
**Solution**
3x + 5 − 5 = 20 − 5
3x = 15
[[3x/3]] = [[15/3]]
**x = 5**
Check: 3(5) + 5 = 20 ✓
## ✏️ Example 7.9
Solve: a) 4x + 1 = 3x + 7 b) 7w + 3 = 2w + 18 c) 5r − 3 = r − 1 d) 20 − 3k = k + 12 e) 6z + 4 = 28
**Solution**
a) 4x − 3x = 7 − 1 ⟹ **x = 6**
b) 7w − 2w = 18 − 3 ⟹ 5w = 15 ⟹ **w = 3**
c) 5r − r = −1 + 3 ⟹ 4r = 2 ⟹ **r =** [[1/2]]
d) 20 − 12 = k + 3k ⟹ 8 = 4k ⟹ **k = 2**
e) 6z = 28 − 4 = 24 ⟹ **z = 4**
> 🎯 **BECE tip** In examinations, always show each step and **check** your answer by substituting it back into the original equation. A check earns confidence — and can catch careless errors.

pages.title: Chapter 7 summary
pages.body:
- An equation states that two expressions are equal; solving finds the value of the unknown.
- Use inverse operations (flag diagram) and keep the equation balanced: do the same to both sides.
- Algebra tiles: x-tiles and unit tiles; zero pairs (+1 and −1) can be added or removed.
- Always check the solution in the original equation.
